source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

gens.text: At the bustling checkpoint, the queue snaked around the barriers, where travelers laid their items in trays. A pat-down was administered, thorough and unyielding. Signs lined the area, instructing travelers to proceed, but the process felt more like an interrogation than a routine check. Instructions were clear, yet the impersonal demeanor of authority left no room for negotiation.

Officers stood ready with their scanning devices, while travelers passed through the metal detectors, their bags and persons divested. Among the lines, a traveler and another were singled out for closer inspection. They presented their documents, and one faced a thorough pat-down. Clear instructions were posted everywhere, signs pointing the way. The impersonal courtesy of authority was maintained, ensuring that every traveler felt seen and secure.

The officer turned to the traveler, holding documents in hand, and began the detailed inspection.
